steps: Open your dominant hand into a five, fingers together and thumb relaxed.
Slide the open hand under your non-dominant flat hand at waist height.
Draw the dominant hand outward and upward from beneath the other hand.
Close the fingers into a flat O as the hand emerges from underneath.
Start with the dominant palm down, letting it rotate as it exits.
tip: As a standalone it means OUT; inside a sentence it usually folds into a classifier verb.

steps: Close your dominant hand into an A fist, thumb resting against the knuckles.
Hold the A fist up at chest height in neutral space.
Start with the palm facing sideways toward your non-dominant side.
Twist the wrist smoothly so the palm finishes facing the floor.
Keep your eyebrows raised slightly, marking it as an open, indefinite offer.
tip: The palm-down twist is the whole sign — hold it sideways and it reads as unfinished.

steps: Shape both hands into flat B handshapes, fingers pressed together and thumbs tucked across the palms.
Hold your non-dominant hand steady at chest height with its palm facing down as the base.
Lift your dominant hand with the palm facing outward, toward the side.
Stroke the dominant hand leftward across the top of the base hand so the two hands brush.
Sweep the dominant hand back rightward along the same path, keeping both hands flat.
Keep your face neutral; using an S-fist instead of a flat base hand is a common regional variant.
tip: Dr. Bill notes BUSINESS likely grew out of WORK — the flat-vs-fist base hand is just variation.

steps: Form the letter W with your dominant hand, spreading your index, middle, and ring fingers upright.
Hold the W at chest height with your palm facing forward.
Move the W through a small sideways arc while keeping the handshape fixed.
Form a second W at the end of the arc, pausing briefly on each letter.
Keep your expression neutral and let the smooth arc carry both letters as one flowing sign.
tip: Lifeprint's preferred production: two Ws with an arc — the same idea as WWW minus one letter.

steps: Open both hands with your fingers spread wide, palms facing inward toward each other.
Hold your hands at chest height about a foot apart in neutral space.
Shuttle both hands forward and backward, trading places as they pass.
Let the tips of your middle fingers brush together on each pass.
Keep the rhythm loose and continuous — never stiff or march-like.
tip: Dr. Bill teaches the INTERNET sign for the concept 'online': recognize the ON+LINE combo, but produce INTERNET.

steps: Make a fist with your non-dominant hand, keeping your thumb sticking straight up.
Hold that fist at chest height with the thumb pointing toward the ceiling.
Extend the index finger of your dominant hand and aim it at the thumb.
Flick the index finger upward so it brushes past the tip of the thumb.
Keep the flick small, quick, and decisive — one sharp upward pass.
Let the index stop at the thumb instead of passing it and the sign still reads as FIRST.
tip: Dr. Bill prefers the flick-past-the-thumb version, but the contact-only version is widely accepted too.

steps: Extend the index finger of your dominant hand, tucking the other fingers into a fist.
Point the fingertip at the center of your chest.
Touch your chest lightly with the fingertip in one short motion.
Keep the touch at chest height and hold a neutral expression.
Drop this sign whenever the verb's direction already shows who is involved.
tip: Often you can drop ME entirely — in ASL the verb's location already shows who is involved.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up, as a steady base.
Shape your dominant hand flat with your fingers pressed together, palm facing down.
Set the edge of the dominant hand across the base palm near the heel.
Slice the dominant hand sideways across the base palm in one smooth stroke.
Keep the base hand perfectly still while the dominant hand does all the work.
tip: Think of slicing off a portion — SOME also covers the concepts part, partial, and portion.

steps: Shape both hands into D letters: index fingers pointing up, other fingers curled in a circle with the thumb.
Hold both hands at chest height with the fingertips aimed straight up.
Bring the two index fingertips together until they touch lightly.
Pull the hands an inch apart, then bring the fingertips together a second time.
Keep the double touch small and quick, like a light double-tap.
tip: Fingertips pointing UP means a romantic date — pointing them forward turns the sign into DESSERT.

steps: Start your dominant hand in a B shape: flat, fingers together, thumb across the palm.
Hold the hand at chest height with the palm facing sideways.
Morph the hand toward a K: narrow the fingers into a V with the thumb up between them.
Flow quickly from B to K, skipping the A and only lightly hinting the C in between.
Let the hand drift slightly backward as the handshape changes.
Aim the palm side of your hand toward whoever will receive what is coming back.
tip: This lexicalized B-(A)-C-K is the general 'return' sense — it is directional, so point it at the receiver.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand upright at chest height, fingers pointing straight up.
Turn that hand's palm sideways, toward your midline, like a standing post.
Shape your dominant hand flat, fingers together, palm facing down.
Rest the flat hand level just above the fingertips of the upright hand.
Let the flat hand mark the highest point, like a roof sitting on a post.
tip: TOP means the highest point, area, or location — for 'the best,' use the separate sign BEST.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand upright at chest height, fingers together and pointing up.
Turn that hand's palm sideways so it stands like a page of paper.
Bend the fingers of your dominant hand at the knuckles, forming a loose bent hand.
Touch the bent fingertips to the top edge of the upright 'paper' hand.
Tap downward along the paper in steps, as if ticking items off a list.
Keep the base hand still while the dominant hand marks each line.
tip: The base hand is the paper and the bent hand marks the items — use the verb TO-LIST for 'make a list.'

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand up at chest height, index and middle fingers extended together.
Extend the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand in the same shape.
Bring the dominant fingers down onto the matching fingers of the base hand.
Tap the base fingers twice with a small, firm double contact.
Keep both palms facing down or angled slightly sideways through the taps.
tip: Double tap for the noun (a name); a single extended contact makes the verb — named, called, christened.

steps: Make an S fist with your dominant hand, fingers curled and thumb across them.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat at chest height, palm up, as a steady base.
Touch the side of the S fist against the middle of the base palm.
Slide the S hand in a small arc down to the lower part of the base palm.
Keep the movement short and controlled, staying in touch with the base hand.
Keep your expression neutral — this is a plain vocabulary sign.
tip: This is the 50-states STATE — 'a state of shock' and 'to state a fact' use entirely different signs.

steps: Shape your non-dominant hand into a C, curving your fingers into a loose tunnel.
Hold the C hand at chest height with its opening facing sideways.
Extend the index finger of your dominant hand, tucking the other fingers away.
Thread the index fingertip straight through the tunnel of the C hand in one pass.
Use a single smooth pass for the verb; repeat the pass for the noun.
tip: Lifeprint marks the old TTY-call E-hand version as do-not-use — the index-through-C version is current.

steps: Raise your dominant hand to chest height in front of you.
Extend your index and middle fingers upward, tucking the rest into a fist.
In isolation, turn your palm to face back toward you.
When counting in a series, turn the palm to face forward instead.
Hold the two fingers upright and steady — no wiggle or extra movement.
tip: Numbers 1 through 5 face you when signed alone but face out when used in a counting series.

steps: Hold both hands flat at chest height, palms facing down, fingers pointing forward.
Start with your dominant hand tucked just behind your non-dominant hand.
Lift the dominant hand up and over in a smooth, level arc.
Land it in front of the non-dominant hand, palms still facing down.
Keep the motion small and symmetrical at chest height.
tip: This NEXT is for 'what's next' — next week, next month, and next year each use their own movement.

steps: Make a flat hand with your dominant hand, keeping all fingers together and straight.
Hold the flat hand out in front of your dominant shoulder, a few inches away.
Move the hand inward toward your shoulder in one smooth, deliberate motion.
Keep your palm facing back toward your shoulder throughout the entire movement.
Keep your face relaxed and your head still; let the backward motion carry the meaning.
tip: Think of reaching back over your shoulder into the past — last week, last time.

steps: Open both hands into loose 5 handshapes, with all fingers comfortably spread apart.
Bend your non-dominant arm to about 45 degrees and hold it across your chest.
Place your dominant 5 hand just behind the non-dominant hand, above the forearm.
Wave the dominant hand back and forth above the arm in a steady rhythm.
Keep the dominant palm facing your chest while the hand waves side to side.
Keep a relaxed, pleasant expression, as if you are enjoying a favorite song.
tip: The waving hand looks like a conductor leading an orchestra through a song.

steps: Make flat hands with both hands, keeping the fingers of each hand together.
Touch your fingertips together in front of your chest, forming a small rooftop shape.
Separate your hands slightly while sliding them sideways to a new spot.
Touch your fingertips together again once the hands reach the new position.
Angle both palms downward and toward each other, keeping the rooftop shape intact.
Keep your expression neutral and your shoulders still; the hands paint the skyline.
tip: The rooftop tap, slide, and tap again traces a row of buildings along a street.

steps: Make an S handshape with both hands by closing each hand into a fist.
Hold your non-dominant fist steady at chest height in front of you.
Place your dominant fist just below the non-dominant fist to start.
Push the dominant fist upward until it meets the underside of the other fist.
Keep both palms facing toward you for the entire upward push.
Nod once with a sincere expression, showing that you stand behind someone.
tip: One fist rising to prop up the other — like holding someone steady.

steps: Make a flat hand with your dominant hand, fingers together and thumb relaxed.
Touch the side of your chin with the fingers of the flat hand.
Slide the hand sideways and off your face in one smooth motion.
Close the moving hand into an A handshape, a fist with the thumb up.
Keep your palm facing sideways as the hand leaves your chin.
Raise your eyebrows slightly and smile to emphasize that this is the very best.
tip: Starts like GOOD at the chin, then pops into a fist — good raised to its highest level.

steps: Make a flat hand with your dominant hand, fingers together and straight.
Touch your lips lightly with the fingertips of the flat hand.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with the palm up.
Move the dominant hand forward and down into the open upturned palm.
Finish with the dominant hand resting in the other palm, both palms up.
Smile warmly as you sign it, matching the positive feeling of the word.
tip: Looks like taking something sweet from your mouth and offering it out — pure good.

steps: Make a G handshape with your dominant hand: index finger and thumb extended upward.
Hold the hand at chest height in the space in front of you.
Raise the hand straight upward to show a tall or lofty height.
Keep the index finger pointing up and the palm facing sideways while rising.
Glance upward along with the rising hand to stress how high it goes.
tip: The rising finger measures the height — like showing how tall a shelf or mountain is.

steps: Shape both hands into loose flat palms, keeping the fingers relaxed and together.
Hold your non-dominant hand steady in front of your chest as the base hand.
Circle your dominant hand above the base hand, then slap it downward and lift it back up a few inches.
Keep both palms facing down throughout the circling and slapping motion.
Keep your expression neutral; repeat the slap once or twice for a natural rhythm.
tip: Initialize it with a U handshape on the dominant hand to mean university specifically; the same sign means college.

steps: Bend the fingers of your dominant hand into a loose claw shape.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with the palm turned up.
Circle the bent fingertips once or twice above the open palm.
Drop the fingertips down to touch the middle of the upturned palm.
Keep your gaze and expression neutral; the sign marks one central spot.
tip: The fingertips landing in the middle of the palm is the giveaway — it is a version of the sign for middle.

steps: Open both hands into fives with the fingers spread wide.
Hold both hands in front of you at about head height, pulled slightly back.
Push both hands forward twice in quick, confident thrusts.
Keep both palms facing forward as the hands travel outward.
Raise your eyebrows and smile to match the enthusiastic meaning.
tip: This is the sign for wonderful — use a modified BIG instead when you mean a large size.

steps: Make an A fist with your dominant hand, thumb sticking up.
Raise the fist near your mouth, as if the thumb were a stamp you just licked.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you like an envelope.
Move the A fist down and press the thumb onto the flat palm.
Keep your expression neutral; the sign also covers a single piece of mail.
tip: Think of licking a stamp and sticking it onto an envelope.

steps: Flatten both hands with the fingers together and extended.
Hold both hands apart in the lower space in front of your torso.
Move both hands forward once in a single smooth push.
Point the fingertips outward with both palms facing each other.
Keep your face neutral; the sign means a method or manner of doing something.
tip: The two hands trace the edges of a path — picture the sides of a road ahead.

steps: Point your dominant index finger upward in a one handshape.
Touch the tip of the index finger to your chin.
Move the finger slightly forward, then sweep it onward in a small arc.
Angle the palm to the side, facing left if you sign right-handed.
Keep a sincere expression; the arc is smaller and softer than the sign for TRUE.
tip: A smaller, softer arc than TRUE — do not punch the finger forward.

steps: Shape both hands into "1" handshapes, extending only the index fingers while the thumbs fold across the palms.
Hold both hands out in front of your chest, with the index fingers angled comfortably at about 45 degrees.
Draw large circles in the air with the tips of your index fingers, moving both hands at the same time.
Circle both hands in the same direction, keeping one hand half a lap ahead of the other, like the hands of a clock.
Keep your face relaxed and neutral; you may pedal the circles forward or backward, but pick one direction.
tip: Both hands circle the SAME direction — never mirrored opposites; think of two race cars on one track, one half a lap ahead.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an "S" fist, folding the fingers down over the thumb.
Hold the fist in front of your chest at a comfortable height, ready to move downward.
Move the whole fist straight downward in one short, smooth motion.
Keep the palm of the fist angled toward your non-dominant side; a palm-down variant is also widely used.
Keep your face neutral and let the downward drop be crisp and deliberate, like pointing at the bottom of a map.
tip: Picture a map: south sits at the bottom, so the S fist drops straight down.

steps: Shape both hands into "10" hands, making fists with the thumbs extended upward.
Hold both hands a bit apart in the space in front of your chest.
Tap the two hands toward each other twice, letting the thumbs briefly bump.
Keep the thumbs facing each other and the palms turned back toward you throughout the taps.
Keep your expression neutral and make the taps light and rhythmic, not forceful.
tip: The two "10" thumbs bump twice — a playful little clash that covers games, sports, and contests.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a clawed "5", spreading the fingers and bending them slightly.
Raise your non-dominant arm a little so the opposite upper arm becomes the target.
Bring the dominant hand down so the clawed fingertips land firmly on the opposite upper arm.
Keep the dominant palm angled down toward the arm as the fingertips strike.
Use a firm, confident expression and tense the shoulders slightly to show force.
tip: The claw strikes the opposite bicep like a power surge — the same production also means powerful.

steps: Shape both hands into horizontal "V" hands, extending the index and middle fingers out sideways.
Stack the dominant "V" hand on top of the non-dominant "V" hand in front of your body.
Move both hands forward together in a small circular motion, repeating the circle twice.
Keep both "V" hands horizontal and stacked, with the fingertips pointing forward as they circle.
Keep a warm, gentle expression; this sign conveys watchful, attentive kindness.
tip: The double forward circle is the giveaway — one circle reads as a cautious, watchful motion instead.

steps: Interlock the fingers of both hands together in front of your chest.
Hold the interlocked hands in the signing space just in front of your torso.
Move both hands together in one big stirring circle, as if stirring a large melting pot.
Keep the wrists loose so the interlocked hands roll smoothly through the whole circle.
Keep your expression neutral; one smooth circle reads as the adjective "American."
tip: The melting-pot stir is the memory hook — interlocked fingers circling like cultures blending together.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a "C", curving the fingers and thumb like a small camera frame.
Hold the "C" hand up at the side of your eye, and raise your non-dominant hand as a flat vertical palm in front of you.
Bring the "C" hand down to touch the flat palm, as if the image you see is captured onto paper.
Keep the flat palm upright and vertical while the "C" hand lands against it.
Keep your gaze and expression neutral; the sign reads as "photo" or "photograph" by context.
tip: C-hand to the eye, then onto the paper — you are framing what you see and printing it.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an L, thumb and index finger held open and steady.
Press the palm of the L hand against the palm of your flat non-dominant hand.
Pull the L hand back an inch or two, dip it down an inch or two, then touch the left palm again.
Keep the L hand's palm facing the non-dominant palm through both contacts.
Sign with a firm, even rhythm and a neutral, serious face.
tip: Change the L to an R for RULE, a P for PRINCIPLE, or a C-to-E change for code of ethics.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a C, all fingers curved together into a claw.
Hold your non-dominant forearm or wrist steady in front of you, palm facing down.
Move the C hand in a small circle over the wrist so its thumb brushes the surface.
Keep the base hand flat, palm down, and still while the C hand circles.
Use quick, compact circles in a small signing space like fluent signers do.
tip: Not the same as CHURCH, which only taps up and down with no circular movement.

steps: Shape both hands into hooked-L claws: index finger hooked like a letter X, thumb extended.
Hold the two claw hands in front of your chest, palms facing each other.
Move both hands outward and apart to show the object's width.
Keep your palms facing each other as the hands separate.
Add the open-mouthed 'cha' mouth shape and a bigger sweep to mean 'huge' or 'enormous'.
tip: The older version used two plain L hands; modern signers hook the index fingers into claws.

steps: Start both hands above head height, fingertips together, a little off to the side.
Move the hands downward toward a spot in front of your torso.
Change both handshapes into bent V hands while the hands descend.
Land the bent V hands in front of your torso to complete the downward path.
Keep the motion smooth, compact, and neutral-faced.
tip: Skip the D-to-L initialized version — some signers consider it Signed English rather than ASL.

steps: Extend your dominant index finger and point it straight downward.
Hold the hand at about waist height in front of your torso.
Move the finger down a short distance, driving the movement from the elbow.
Keep your palm facing in toward your body while the finger points down.
A firm single downward stroke reads as 'down'; watch for added meanings like 'downstairs' or 'depressed'.
tip: The same downward point can mean 'here', 'foot', or 'something below you' — context decides.

steps: Extend your dominant index finger, keeping the other fingers closed.
Point directly at the person, or at the spot where you set them up in your signing space.
Hold the point briefly toward their location — that single point is the whole sign.
Keep your palm facing down or slightly to the side while pointing.
Direct your eye gaze toward the person as you point, with a neutral face.
tip: HE, SHE, HIM, and HER all use the same index point — the surrounding sentence tells the meaning.

steps: Hold up your dominant hand with thumb, index, and middle fingers extended.
Keep the hand upright at chest height with your palm facing forward.
Spread the three extended fingers slightly apart so they read clearly.
Keep your palm facing forward and your fingers pointing up.
Hold the handshape steady with a neutral face for the citation form of the number three.
tip: Use thumb plus index and middle fingers — not index, middle, and ring.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and steady in front of you.
Place your dominant hand at the near end of the non-dominant hand's top edge.
Move the dominant hand along the top edge until it reaches the far end and falls off.
Keep your palms angled naturally toward each other through the path.
Make the drop-off at the edge quick and decisive, with a matter-of-fact face.
tip: Use FINISH for actions that end ('movie finished'); this sign is for 'the end' of a thing itself.

steps: Shape both hands into Y handshapes, thumb and pinky extended outward.
Hold both Y hands in front of your body at about waist level.
Move both hands downward a short distance together.
Angle your palms inward toward your body, or slightly upward, during the drop.
Keep the motion firm and your face neutral — it reads as 'right now, currently'.
tip: Same sign as NOW and TODAY — Lifeprint groups 'present, current, today' under one sign.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of your torso, palm facing down.
Curve the hand slightly so it acts like a doorway or barrier.
Sweep your dominant hand under it, entering at the thumb side and exiting at the pinky side.
Let the dominant hand pass through as if a small animal slipping under a wall.
Mouth the English word 'access' while signing — the mouthing is what makes it read as ACCESS rather than ENTER.
tip: There is no separate citation sign: fluent signers do ENTER twice while mouthing 'access', or fingerspell A-C-C-E-S-S.

steps: Shape both index fingers into slightly bent hooks, keeping your other fingers folded down.
Touch the tips of the bent fingers to your upper chest or shoulders, one on each side.
Sweep both hands forward and downward in one smooth arc, finishing in front of your chest.
Begin with both palms facing down and let them roll to face upward as you finish.
Keep a neutral expression; the arc traces the stretch of time from then until now.
tip: Picture a timeline on your body: the sign starts back at your shoulders (the past) and lands in the present.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a G, pinching the thumb against the side of the bent index finger.
Hold the G hand up beside your temple, a few inches out from the side of your head.
Draw one small circle in the air beside your temple with the G hand.
Finish the circle by touching the fingertips of the G hand lightly to your temple.
Angle the G so the fingertips point toward your head; keep your expression calm and neutral.
tip: The circle at the temple marks the seat of power; swapping the G for an F signs federal.

steps: Extend both index fingers, folding your other fingers down against your palms.
Hold both hands in front of your chest, with the index fingers pointing forward.
Trace a square in the air, drawing each side with your index fingertips.
Keep the fingertips aimed forward as you outline all four sides of the square.
Keep a neutral expression; the traced outline stands for a board, sign, or billboard.
tip: Trace the shape of a classroom whiteboard; sign WHITE or BLACK first to say whiteboard or blackboard.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a flat hand, letting the fingers bend down just a little.
Imagine two small children standing in front of you, one a little to your left and one to your right.
Pat the top of the first imaginary child's head once with your flat hand.
Shift your hand sideways and pat the top of the second imaginary child's head once.
Keep your palm facing down through both pats and your face warm and natural.
tip: Two quick head-pats read as children; one head-pat means a single child.

steps: Shape both hands into hooked X hands, bending the index fingers like small hooks.
Hold both hands in front of your chest with the backs of the hands nearly touching.
Twist both wrists in opposite directions, as if wringing out a small cloth.
Let the palms swing toward and then away from each other as the wrists roll.
Keep a neutral expression; the twisting hands picture something becoming different.
tip: The wring-like twist is the heart of the sign; the same motion also covers exchange and trade-like swapping.

steps: Shape both hands into flattened O hands, touching each fingertip to its thumb.
Hold both hands in front of your chest, a few inches apart at stomach-to-chest height.
Rotate both wrists forward together, rolling the hands over twice in smooth turns.
Keep both palms angled downward as the hands complete the two forward rolls.
Keep your face relaxed; the rolling motion suggests goods turning over on shelves.
tip: The same production also means store; make both wrist rolls clear so the sign reads cleanly.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a loose fist, keeping the wrist relaxed.
Hold the hand in front of your torso at about chest height.
Sweep the hand backward over your dominant shoulder in one smooth arc.
Keep your palm facing inward toward your body through the sweep.
Enlarge the sweep for "long ago" and shrink it for "just a moment ago."
tip: Lifeprint groups PAST, before, and previously under this one over-the-shoulder sign.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a flattened O, thumb and fingertips nearly touching.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of your torso, palm facing up.
Slap the flattened O hand down onto the flat palm once or twice.
Keep the base palm facing up and steady while the dominant hand taps it.
Finish with a neutral face — the tapping motion carries the meaning.
tip: Think of a hand dropping coins onto an open palm — the slap is the key movement.

steps: Close your dominant hand into a firm fist.
Touch the side of the fist or knuckles against your chin.
Pull the fist straight downward from the chin toward your chest.
Keep the fist closed through the whole downward pull.
Imagine stroking a long beard as you move — the image locks in the meaning.
tip: Looks like AGE, but AGE starts as an open O at the chin while OLD stays a fist.

steps: Shape both hands into flat B handshapes, fingers together and straight.
Rest the edge of your dominant hand on the top of the non-dominant hand.
Slide the dominant hand forward off the base hand in one smooth motion.
Angle the non-dominant palm to the right and the dominant palm to the left.
Keep the base hand perfectly still — only the dominant hand moves.
tip: Lifeprint lists it as MAJOR — the same sign covers main, profession, career, and field of work.

steps: Shape both hands into V handshapes, index and middle fingers extended.
Hold the V hands up near your eyes, fingertips pointing forward.
Move both hands outward and forward away from your face together.
Keep both palms facing inward toward your face as the hands travel.
Aim the movement toward the person or place being visited.
tip: The sign is directional — where the hands travel shows who visits whom.

steps: Touch your dominant thumb and index fingertip together, other fingers relaxed.
Hold the hand in front of your chin or chest.
Flick the thumb outward off the index finger, like flipping a coin.
Keep the palm facing inward toward you while the thumb flicks.
Pair it with a slight squint or pursed lips to stress "a tiny amount."
tip: Same sign as LITTLE-BIT — the tiny flicking motion is the whole message.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a V, extending your index and middle fingers while folding the others down.
Make a firm fist with your non-dominant hand and hold it up in front of your chest.
Bring your V-hand fingers down so they slap firmly against the back of your non-dominant fist.
Use one firm slap for the verb meaning store up; slap twice when you mean the noun storage.
Keep your palm angled sideways through the motion and your expression calm and neutral.
tip: The V fingers landing on the fist picture putting something away for safekeeping — one slap saves it, two slaps mean storage.

steps: Shape both hands into flat open hands, holding your fingers together and fully extended.
Raise your dominant flat hand to chest height and hold your non-dominant flat hand lower, near your waist.
Move your dominant hand straight downward until it lands just above the lower hand, shrinking the gap between them.
Keep your dominant palm facing down and your non-dominant palm facing up to meet it.
Keep your expression neutral; the shrinking gap shows the amount sitting low.
tip: The gap between the hands is the amount — a tiny gap means low; the L-initialized version is Signed English, so stick with this one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand upright in front of your chest with your fingers together.
Pinch your dominant thumb and index finger together to mark the width of a newspaper column.
Draw your pinched fingers straight down the face of your base hand's palm, from top to bottom.
Angle your dominant palm toward the base hand as your fingers travel downward.
Keep your face neutral; the same production also signs chapter, column, or a newspaper section.
tip: Sign NEWSPAPER first when you mean a news article, or RESEARCH first for a research article.

steps: Extend the index fingers of both hands, folding your other fingers down against your palms.
Hold both hands up in front of your chest with the index fingers a few inches apart.
Trace the outline of a rectangle in the air with your index fingertips, sizing it to the card.
Keep both palms facing each other as your fingertips draw each side of the rectangle.
Keep your face neutral; the same outline also signs a check, an envelope, or a brick.
tip: Size the rectangle to the object — a small rectangle for a credit card, a larger one for an envelope.

steps: Shape your non-dominant hand into a flattened O, pressing your fingertips together against your thumb.
Extend the index finger of your dominant hand, folding your other fingers down into a fist.
Hold your flattened O hand steady in front of your chest as the fixed center point.
Move your dominant index finger in a full circle around the O hand, tracing its outer edge.
Keep your palm facing sideways through the circle and your expression neutral.
tip: The circling finger travels around the fixed O — picture a small planet orbiting the sun.

steps: Extend the index fingers of both hands, folding your other fingers down against your palms.
Hold both index fingers upright in front of your chest with your palms facing outward.
Cross the two index fingers at their middles so they form a small X shape.
Twist the crossed fingers outward so the fingertips swing apart to opposite sides.
Use a larger, firmer twist than you would for BUT; keep your expression neutral or emphatic.
tip: Keep BUT small and make DIFFERENT big — a tiny motion reads as but, a wide twist reads as different.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a G, pinching your thumb and index finger into a small pincer.
Extend the index finger of your non-dominant hand and hold it up in front of your chest.
Tap the side of your dominant G hand once against the side of your non-dominant index finger.
Angle your dominant palm toward the non-dominant hand and the non-dominant palm back toward it.
Use a single tap for the verb print; tap twice to sign the noun newspaper.
tip: Think of a printing press stamping paper — one tap prints, two taps name the newspaper.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a slightly curved cup, letting your fingers relax and curve gently.
Hold the curved hand up in front of your chest in neutral signing space.
Twist the hand once at the wrist, rotating it through a single smooth turn.
Let your palm orientation roll with the twist instead of holding it fixed.
Purse your lips and narrow your eyes slightly, as if studying two things side by side.
tip: Lifeprint teaches COMPARE with the same production as SEEM — one deliberate twist; a double twist leans toward seemingly.

steps: Hold both hands flat with the fingers together, palms facing each other at chest height.
Move your flat hands apart to show the two opposite walls of the room.
Bend both hands at the knuckles so they form right angles like bent frames.
Bring the bent hands back toward each other to trace the front and back walls.
Keep your palms angled inward so the hands sketch a small square room floating in the air.
Hold a neutral expression — context decides whether this shape means ROOM or BOX.
tip: Same sign as BOX — draw a little box in the air, and the sentence tells people which word you mean.

steps: Hold both flat hands up with the palms facing each other at chest height.
Separate the flat hands sideways to show the two walls of the box.
Bend both hands at the knuckles into right-angle shapes.
Move the bent hands toward each other to mark the front and back of the box.
Angle your palms inward so the hands outline a small box floating in front of you.
Keep a plain expression — the identical sign means ROOM when the topic is a room.
tip: Lifeprint teaches this as the identical sign to ROOM, and it also works inside BEDROOM (BED + this sign).

steps: Hold your non-dominant index finger upright in front of your chest.
Make a fist with your dominant hand, the thumb resting along the side like an A handshape.
Press the thumb side of the fist against the top edge of the upright index finger.
Brush the fist back and forth along the finger two or three times, as if polishing a shoe.
Keep both palms facing sideways while the brushing stays short and quick.
Stay relaxed and neutral — swap the A fist for a T fist only if you must mark the English word.
tip: Think polishing your skills — Lifeprint says the plain PRACTICE form usually carries the training meaning on its own.

steps: Make the sign MAN: open your dominant hand, fingers together pointing straight up.
Touch your thumb to your forehead, then draw the hand straight down to your chest.
Finish with the thumb resting on your chest and the fingers still pointing upward.
Now open both hands into relaxed curved-5 shapes with the palms facing slightly forward.
Slide both hands forward while twisting the palms slightly backward, as if cupping a large ball.
Keep your face neutral — the added group marker is what turns MAN into MEN.
tip: Lifeprint's own example: MAN plus the CLUSTER/group sign means 'men' — that group sign alone can also mean team, category, or collection.

steps: Shape both hands into open F handshapes, thumb and index forming loose circles.
Hold the two F hands apart in front of your chest with the palms facing each other.
Bring the hands together so the two F circles interlock like links of a chain.
Tug the linked hands gently outward once to show the connection holds firm.
Keep your fingers relaxed so the link reads as two small rings hooking together.
Wear a purposeful, neutral expression — this is the 'connect two things together' version of JOIN.
tip: Two F hands hooking like chain links — Lifeprint uses this same production for CONNECT, LINK, and 'join two things together'.

steps: Pinch your dominant index finger against your thumb tip, like gripping a small token.
Hold the pinched fingers out in front of your chest with the palm facing down.
Close the pinch on an imaginary option and lift the hand upward toward yourself.
Draw the hand back to your body in one smooth, decisive sweep.
Keep the wrist steady and the palm facing down through the whole pull-in motion.
Nod once as you finish — selecting is a firm and deliberate choice.
tip: SELECT is signed exactly like CHOOSE — Lifeprint glosses this same production as CHOOSE-[select].

steps: Shape both hands into T handshapes, each index finger laid across the top of its thumb.
Touch the fingertips of both T hands together in front of your chest.
Circle both hands outward together, tracing a wide loop like teammates around a table.
Bring the hands back around so the fingertips meet again at the center.
Keep the two hands mirroring each other through the entire circle.
Stay warm and neutral — the circle reads as a group, and the T hands say team.
tip: Same circle as FAMILY and CLASS, just with T hands — this dictionary's FAMILY entry confirms the initialized pattern.

steps: Open both hands into relaxed curved-5 shapes, fingers loosely curled like soft claws.
Hold the hands up at chest height with the palms facing slightly forward.
Push both hands forward together in one smooth motion.
As the hands travel, twist both wrists so the palms turn slightly backward.
Imagine sliding your hands around the sides of a large invisible ball.
Keep your expression neutral — this GROUP sign doubles as CATEGORY, CLASS, or COLLECTION.
tip: Lifeprint notes this GROUP/CLUSTER sign can be labeled CATEGORY — use it when sorting things into labeled sets.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a W, three fingers up and the thumb holding the pinky.
Hold the W in front of your chest at a comfortable height, palm angled slightly forward.
Sweep the whole hand sideways to your left in one short, level motion.
Keep the W handshape frozen and the palm steady through the sweep.
Picture a map: west sits at the left edge, so the W travels toward it.
Keep your face neutral and the movement crisp — direction signs stay small and clear.
tip: Map logic: the W travels leftward, just as SOUTH's S drops downward — Lifeprint notes a few signers move the W rightward instead.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a G, index finger and thumb held parallel and close.
Bring the G hand up to your chin area, fingertips pointing slightly outward.
Tap or brush the chin once with the G handshape in a small, quick motion.
Keep the movement light — one touch, not a repeated rubbing.
Hold the handshape steady so the G stays readable through the tap.
Sign with a relaxed, respectful expression — this is a straightforward identity sign.
tip: A G hand tapped at the chin — Lifeprint's own usage; regional variants exist, so mirror your local Deaf community.

steps: Make an A handshape with both hands: a fist with the thumb resting along the side.
Stack the hands at your chest with your dominant fist resting on your non-dominant fist.
Thrust both hands straight up once with one large, quick upward movement.
End with the hands floating an inch or two off your chest, palms still facing in.
Keep a neutral expression — the double-tap version of this sign means ADDRESS instead.
tip: One big upward push says you LIVE somewhere; two small taps of the same sign would mean the noun ADDRESS.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and horizontal in front of you as the tabletop.
Make a flat hand with your dominant hand, fingers together, palm facing down.
Lay the dominant hand on top of the non-dominant hand to show the flat top surface.
Pat the base hand twice with short downward taps of the dominant hand.
Keep the base hand steady while the taps sketch out the flat tabletop.
tip: This one sign covers both TABLE and DESK; some signers initialize it with a D hand, but Lifeprint keeps the plain flat-top version.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand upright with the fingers together, like a screen edge.
Spread all five fingers of your dominant hand into a 5 handshape.
Press the dominant hand against the edge of the upright hand so it can pivot.
Twist your dominant wrist side to side while it stays pressed to the base hand.
Keep the twisting small and quick, as if film frames were flickering past.
Stay neutral-faced — the same sign is used for a video as well as a movie.
tip: Lifeprint teaches the upright base hand as version one; many signers instead lay the base hand flat, palm down — both are understood.

steps: Hold a flat hand with the fingers together near your mouth, not quite touching it.
Start with the palm angled toward your face, as if beginning the sign GOOD.
Sweep the hand outward to the right while closing into an A fist with a loose thumb.
End with the fist out in front, thumb side up and palm facing left.
Keep the movement smooth and quick; exaggerate it to mean 'way better'.
tip: Think GOOD + ER — Lifeprint teaches BETTER as a fancier version of GOOD, and BEST goes even bigger and upward.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat with the palm facing up in front of you.
Make an R handshape with your dominant hand, crossing the middle finger over the index.
Lay the R hand across the palm-side of the base hand's fingers.
Lift the R, slide it about two inches toward the heel of the palm, and lay it down again.
Use a double motion — lay, lift-and-shift, lay — to complete the sign.
tip: The SIGNATURE sign, a small scribbling motion, is often used in place of this initialized R version to mean register.

steps: Extend your non-dominant hand in front of you in a flat handshape, palm up.
Make an X handshape with your dominant hand — a fist with a bent index finger — palm facing back.
Bring the bent index finger down to strike the palm of the base hand.
Use one sharp downward tap of the X finger against the palm.
Keep a neutral expression — this sign also covers fee, fine, and sometimes tax.
tip: Asking what something is worth uses a different sign: two F hands tapping together at the fingertips, like the sign IMPORTANT.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat with the palm facing up in front of your chest.
Extend your dominant index finger straight up in a 1 handshape.
Rest the fingertip on the heel of the base hand's palm so your wrist can pivot.
Give one very quick small tick with the fingertip, moving only from the wrist.
Keep the tick tiny and fast — the same sign done slower and larger means MINUTE.
tip: When minutes and seconds both appear in one sentence, sign MINUTE and spell S-E-C to keep them clear.

steps: Extend your dominant index finger straight up in a 1 handshape.
Place the fingertip against your lips, with your palm facing left.
Move the finger straight forward several inches with one quick motion.
Give a firm nod as the finger moves forward to stress that it is true.
Land with the finger out in front; this is the sign TRUE carrying the meaning REALLY.
tip: Lifeprint notes TRUE covers really, surely, and indeed — and ASL often builds 'really' into the other sign itself instead of signing it alone.

steps: Make a flat handshape with your non-dominant hand, fingers together and pointing straight up.
Hold the upright flat hand at chest height with the palm facing toward you.
Raise your dominant hand into a matching flat handshape, fingers together and extended.
Move the dominant flat hand toward the non-dominant palm from your dominant side.
Strike the palm of the dominant hand against the non-dominant palm in one firm contact.
Keep your brows lowered and your expression firm — opposition lives in the face too.
tip: Two palms colliding means opposition — Lifeprint notes the same sign also covers 'anti' and suing someone.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an S handshape, thumb pressed across the curled fingers.
Touch the side of the S hand to one side of your chest, fingertips facing inward.
As you move across your chest, let the S handshape open into an F handshape.
Land the F hand on the other side of your chest with a second firm touch.
Do not drag the hand across — make two separate contacts, one on each side.
Keep your face neutral; most signers start on the non-dominant side of the chest.
tip: Same two-touch chest pattern as MEMBER and COMMITTEE — the S-to-F handshape change is what makes it STAFF.

steps: Raise both hands to the sides of your head with your fingers loosely curved and spread.
Angle your palms inward toward each other, holding the hands about shoulder-width apart.
Keep your elbows relaxed and low so the hands frame the space beside your temples.
Trace small circles in the air with both hands at the same time.
Keep the motion tight and close to your head, as if outlining the subject you are naming.
Wear a plain, neutral expression — the same sign doubles as QUOTE, SUBJECT, and TITLE.
tip: The same production works for quote, subject, title, and 'about' — Lifeprint teaches it as 'the subject of an article or book.'

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of your chest, fingers together pointing to your dominant side.
Lay your dominant flat hand on top of the base hand, starting near its wrist.
Slide the dominant hand along the top of the base hand toward the fingertips.
Let the dominant hand fall off the edge when it reaches the end of the base hand.
Keep the base hand still and palm-down — it is the ground the traveling hand crosses.
Hold a neutral face — the same production signs END and 'conclusion of.'
tip: One hand slides off the other — Lifeprint glosses this production as 'end / complete / conclusion of.'

steps: Close both hands into loose fists with the thumbs resting up on top.
Hold the fists at chest height, about a shoulder-width apart in neutral space.
Turn your palms to face each other so the two fists mirror one another.
Push both hands straight forward together in one smooth, level motion.
Keep the fist shapes frozen while they travel, as if paving a stretch of road.
Stay neutral-faced — the same production signs WAY, PATH, and ROAD.
tip: Two fists pushing forward pave the road — Lifeprint: one sign covers street, way, path, and road.
